variants.stem: During the depolarization phase of a neuron's action potential, which ion rushes into the cell?
A resting neuron is stimulated enough to reach threshold and voltage-gated channels open. Which ion flows inward?
The rising phase of an action potential happens because positive charge enters the cell. Which ion carries that charge?
Which ion's inward movement makes the inside of a neuron less negative at the start of an action potential?
Depolarization of a nerve cell membrane is caused mainly by an influx of which ion?
In the first stage of nerve conduction, the inside of the membrane becomes positive. This is caused by the entry of which ion?
Which statement correctly identifies the ion that enters a neuron during depolarization?
Local anesthetics stop nerve impulses by blocking voltage-gated channels for which ion?

questions.why: Depolarization occurs when voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ flows into the neuron, making the inside of the cell more positive.
questions.deep: Repolarization follows as Na⁺ channels close and K⁺ channels open, letting K⁺ flow out. Memory aid: Sodium Surges in, Potassium Pours out. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump later restores the resting concentration gradients.

variants.stem: In a simple withdrawal reflex, such as pulling a hand away from a hot stove, which structure processes the signal and sends the response?
Which structure acts as the integration center in a reflex arc?
A patient's knee jerks when the patellar tendon is tapped. Where is this response coordinated?
In a reflex arc, the sensory neuron synapses with an interneuron located in which structure?
Where is the integration center for most somatic reflexes located?
opts: Gray matter of the spinal cord

variants.stem: Reflexes are faster than conscious reactions because the signal is processed mainly in which structure?
Which of the following sits between the sensory neuron and the motor neuron in a spinal reflex arc?
You jerk your hand back from a sharp object before you feel any pain. Which structure handled that rapid response?

questions.why: In a spinal reflex, the sensory neuron synapses with an interneuron in the spinal cord, which activates a motor neuron. The brain is informed afterward.
questions.deep: Reflex arc order: receptor → sensory (afferent) neuron → integration center (spinal cord) → motor (efferent) neuron → effector. Afferent = arrives at the CNS; efferent = exits the CNS. Because the cerebral cortex is bypassed, reflexes are faster than voluntary responses.

variants.stem: Which brain structure controls involuntary functions such as breathing rate and heart rate?
Damage to which brain structure would most directly threaten the control of respiration and heart rhythm?
Which region connects the brain to the spinal cord and regulates reflexes such as vomiting, coughing, and sneezing?
Breathing continues during sleep without conscious effort. Which brain structure primarily drives this automatic rhythm?
Which structure is the primary control center for heart rate, blood vessel diameter, and breathing?
The part of the brainstem that continues into the spinal cord and contains the cardiovascular and respiratory centers is the:
Which brain structure controls vital autonomic rhythms rather than movement coordination or reasoning?
Which brain region contains the cardiac, respiratory, and vasomotor centers?

questions.why: The medulla oblongata contains the centers that automatically regulate heart rate, breathing, and blood vessel diameter.
questions.deep: The brainstem consists of the midbrain, pons, and medulla. The cerebrum handles conscious thought and voluntary movement, while the cerebellum coordinates balance and smooth movement. Memory aid: Medulla = Maintains life functions.

variants.stem: Which chamber pumps oxygen-rich blood into the aorta for distribution to the body?
Which heart chamber has the thickest muscular wall because it must generate enough pressure for systemic circulation?
Blood leaves the heart through the aortic valve. From which chamber does it come?
Which chamber sends blood into the systemic circuit rather than the pulmonary circuit?
The mitral valve opens and blood fills a chamber that then contracts to eject blood into the aorta. Which chamber is it?
Contraction of which chamber produces the pulse that can be felt at the wrist?
Which chamber of the heart does the most work with each heartbeat?
Which chamber ejects blood at the highest pressure?

questions.why: The left ventricle ejects oxygenated blood into the aorta, so it must produce the highest pressure and has the thickest wall.
questions.deep: The right ventricle only pumps to the nearby lungs (low pressure), while the left ventricle pushes blood through the whole body. Path: left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta. Atria receive blood; ventricles pump it out.

variants.stem: Which structure is known as the natural pacemaker of the heart?
Where does the electrical impulse that starts each normal heartbeat originate?
The conduction pathway of the heart begins in the wall of the right atrium at which structure?
Which structure normally sets the resting heart rate at about 60 to 100 beats per minute?
On an ECG, the P wave represents atrial depolarization triggered by impulses from which structure?
Which part of the cardiac conduction system depolarizes fastest on its own and therefore sets the pace?
An artificial pacemaker is implanted to take over the job of which natural structure?
Which cluster of specialized cardiac cells starts the impulse that spreads across both atria?

questions.why: The SA node, located in the right atrial wall, depolarizes fastest and starts each heartbeat, so it is the heart's pacemaker.
questions.deep: Conduction order: SA node → atria contract → AV node (brief delay) → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers → ventricles contract. Memory aid: SA = Starts Alright. If the SA node fails, the AV node can take over at a slower rate.

variants.stem: Which structure of the nephron is the site where blood is filtered under pressure?
The first step of urine formation, filtration, occurs across a tuft of capillaries. What is this structure called?
Large proteins and blood cells normally stay in the blood because the filtration barrier of which structure blocks them?
Which part of the nephron receives blood from the afferent arteriole and filters it?
Filtration, reabsorption, and secretion are the three steps of urine formation. Which structure carries out filtration?
Which nephron structure is a ball of capillaries?
High blood pressure in the afferent arteriole pushes fluid out of the blood across which structure?
Within the renal corpuscle, which structure is the site of blood filtration?

questions.why: The glomerulus is a cluster of capillaries where blood pressure forces water and small solutes out of the blood into the nephron.
questions.deep: The nephron is the whole functional unit; the glomerulus is just its filtering part. Flow of filtrate: Bowman's capsule → proximal tubule → loop of Henle → distal tubule → collecting duct. Most reabsorption happens in the proximal tubule, not the glomerulus.

variants.stem: During muscle contraction, which protein's heads attach to actin to form cross-bridges?
Which protein makes up the thick filaments of a sarcomere?
In the sliding filament model, which protein pulls the thin filaments toward the center of the sarcomere?
Which protein uses ATP to perform the power stroke during contraction?
A cross-bridge forms when a protein head binds to a thin filament. Which protein has that head?
Which filament protein has globular heads that extend toward actin?
Of the two main contractile proteins in skeletal muscle, which one forms the thick filaments?
ATPase activity in the heads of which protein supplies the energy for the power stroke?

questions.why: Myosin forms the thick filaments, and its heads bind actin and use ATP to pull the thin filaments inward, shortening the sarcomere.
questions.deep: Sliding filament steps: Ca²⁺ binds troponin, tropomyosin shifts and exposes binding sites on actin, myosin heads attach (cross-bridge), then pivot (power stroke) using ATP. Memory aid: Myosin = Mover (thick), Actin = Anchor-track (thin).

variants.stem: Which cell type secretes large quantities of antibodies?
After a B lymphocyte is activated, it differentiates into which antibody-producing cell?
Which of these cells is derived from activated B cells and makes antibodies?
Which cell is the main antibody factory of humoral immunity?
Humoral immunity depends on antibodies released into the blood. Which cell actually releases them?
Which cell has abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum because it manufactures and exports antibodies?
Which cell results when a B cell meets its antigen and receives help from a helper T cell?
Which cell is responsible for producing and secreting antibodies after exposure to an antigen?

questions.why: When a B cell is activated by its antigen (usually with help from a helper T cell), it becomes a plasma cell that secretes antibodies.
questions.deep: B cells mature in bone marrow; T cells mature in the thymus. Some activated B cells become memory B cells instead, which allow a faster response on re-exposure. Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells directly rather than making antibodies.

variants.stem: Which section of the small intestine receives chyme directly from the stomach?
Where do bile and pancreatic juice enter the small intestine?
Which segment of the small intestine is the shortest and lies immediately after the pylorus?
Chyme leaves the stomach through the pyloric sphincter and first enters which structure?
Which is the first of the three sections of the small intestine?
Chemical digestion in the small intestine begins in which segment, where secretions from the liver and pancreas are added?
The common bile duct and pancreatic duct empty into which part of the digestive tract?
Which segment of the small intestine lies between the stomach and the jejunum?

questions.why: Chyme passes from the stomach through the pyloric sphincter into the duodenum, the first segment of the small intestine, where bile and pancreatic juice are added.
questions.deep: Order: duodenum → jejunum → ileum. Most chemical digestion occurs in the duodenum, most nutrient absorption in the jejunum, and the ileum absorbs vitamin B₁₂ and bile salts. The ileocecal valve joins the ileum to the large intestine.

variants.stem: Select all that apply: Which of the following belong to the axial skeleton?
Select all that apply: Which of these are part of the axial skeleton?
Select all that apply: The axial skeleton forms the central axis of the body. Which bones fall into this group?
Select all that apply: Which of these structures are NOT part of the appendicular skeleton?
Select all that apply: Which of these protect the brain or the organs of the thorax and belong to the axial skeleton?
Select all that apply: Which are components of the axial skeleton?
Select all that apply: Which of the following belong to the axial skeleton rather than the appendicular skeleton?
Select all that apply: Which of the following are classified as part of the axial skeleton?

questions.why: The axial skeleton consists of the skull, vertebral column, ribs, and sternum. The limbs and the girdles that attach them form the appendicular skeleton.
questions.deep: Memory aid: Axial = the body's axis (central line); Appendicular = appendages (arms and legs) plus the girdles that connect them. The shoulder (pectoral) girdle is the scapula and clavicle; the pelvic girdle is the hip bones. Common traps: ribs are axial, and the pelvic girdle is appendicular.

variants.stem: Tap the left atrium. (This view faces the patient, so the patient's left appears on the right side of the image.)
Tap the chamber that receives oxygenated blood returning from the lungs.
Tap the chamber that receives blood from the pulmonary veins.
Tap the upper chamber on the patient's left side. (The patient's left appears on the right side of the image.)
Tap the atrium that empties through the mitral valve into the left ventricle.
Tap the receiving chamber that holds freshly oxygenated blood just before it enters the ventricle that supplies the aorta.
Tap the thin-walled receiving chamber of the left side of the heart. (The patient's left appears on the right side of the image.)
Tap the atrium that sends blood on to the left ventricle.

questions.why: The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary veins and passes it through the mitral valve to the left ventricle.
questions.deep: In an anterior diagram the patient's left is on your right. Blue/dark blue chambers show the oxygen-poor right side and red chambers the oxygen-rich left side. Memory aid: the Left Atrium Lands the lung blood (pulmonary veins), and the right atrium receives the body's blood via the vena cavae.

variants.stem: Which process copies a gene's DNA sequence into messenger RNA?
RNA polymerase builds an mRNA strand using DNA as a template. What is this process called?
In eukaryotic cells, mRNA is first made in the nucleus. Which process produces it?
Which step of gene expression produces a single-stranded RNA copy of a DNA template?
Which is the first step of gene expression, the flow of information from a gene toward a protein?
If a cell needs to make a protein, which process must first occur in the nucleus to create the mRNA message?
Which process produces an mRNA strand in which uracil pairs with adenine on the DNA template?
Which term describes the synthesis of RNA from a DNA template?

questions.why: Transcription is the process in which RNA polymerase copies a gene's DNA sequence into mRNA, taking place in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells.
questions.deep: DNA → (transcription) → mRNA → (translation) → protein. Memory aid: transcription = same 'language' (nucleic acid to nucleic acid), translation = changing language (nucleotides to amino acids) at the ribosome. In RNA, uracil replaces thymine.

variants.stem: Which type of cell division produces four genetically different haploid cells?
Gametes (sperm and egg cells) are produced by which process?
Which process reduces the chromosome number by half, going from diploid to haploid?
Crossing over and independent assortment increase genetic variation during which process?
A diploid cell with 46 chromosomes divides to make cells with 23 chromosomes each. Which process is this?
Which process involves two successive divisions and results in four daughter cells?
Germ cells in the testes and ovaries divide by which process to form haploid gametes?
Which process results in daughter cells that are not genetically identical to the parent and have half as many chromosomes?

questions.why: Meiosis consists of two divisions that turn one diploid cell into four genetically unique haploid cells (gametes).
questions.deep: Mitosis: one division, two identical diploid body (somatic) cells, used for growth and repair. Meiosis: two divisions, four unique haploid cells, used for reproduction. Crossing over (prophase I) and independent assortment create the genetic diversity.

variants.stem: Two heterozygous parents (Aa × Aa) have children. What percent of their offspring are expected to be homozygous recessive (aa)? Give a whole number.
In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant over short (t). Two heterozygous tall plants are crossed. What percent of the offspring are expected to be short? Give a whole number.
Both parents carry one dominant and one recessive allele for a trait. What is the probability, as a percent, that a child inherits two recessive alleles? Give a whole number.
A Punnett square crosses Bb × Bb. What percent of the offspring are expected to have the genotype bb? Give a whole number.
Two brown-eyed parents are both heterozygous (Bb), where brown is dominant over blue (b). What percent of their children are expected to have blue eyes? Give a whole number.
In a monohybrid cross between two hybrid organisms (Ee × Ee), what percent of offspring are expected to be homozygous for the recessive allele? Give a whole number.
Two unaffected parents each carry one copy of a recessive disease allele. What percent chance does each child have of being affected? Give a whole number.
A cross between two heterozygous plants gives a Punnett square with four boxes. What percent of the boxes show the homozygous recessive genotype? Give a whole number.

questions.why: A heterozygous × heterozygous cross (Aa × Aa) gives 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, so 1 of 4 offspring (25%) is homozygous recessive.
questions.deep: Genotype ratio is 1:2:1 and phenotype ratio is 3:1 (dominant:recessive) for a monohybrid hybrid cross. Homozygous = two identical alleles (AA or aa); heterozygous = two different alleles (Aa). Probability = favorable boxes ÷ total boxes.

variants.stem: Which feature do prokaryotic cells lack?
What is the main structural difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
Bacteria are prokaryotes. Which structure is absent from bacterial cells?
In a eukaryotic cell, DNA is stored inside a membrane-bound compartment. Which cells lack this compartment?
Which structure is found in eukaryotic cells but not in bacteria?
Prokaryotic DNA is found in a region called the nucleoid. What does this indicate about the cell?
Which cell type has its genetic material free in the cytoplasm rather than enclosed in a nucleus?
Which statement comparing eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells is true?
opts: Only eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus
Only prokaryotes have a plasma membrane

questions.why: Prokaryotic cells have no membrane-bound nucleus or other membrane-bound organelles; their DNA sits in the cytoplasm in a region called the nucleoid.
questions.deep: Prokaryotes (bacteria, archaea) are generally smaller and simpler. Eukaryotes (animals, plants, fungi, protists) have a nucleus and organelles such as mitochondria and the Golgi apparatus. Both types have DNA, ribosomes, cytoplasm, and a plasma membrane.

variants.stem: Which organelle contains digestive enzymes that break down worn-out cell parts and ingested material?
A cell engulfs a bacterium. Which organelle fuses with the vesicle to digest it?
Which organelle is often called the cell's recycling and waste-disposal center?
Which organelle is filled with hydrolytic enzymes that work best in an acidic interior?
Which organelle breaks down macromolecules such as proteins, lipids, and carbohydrates inside the cell?
Old or damaged organelles are digested inside which membrane-bound sac?
White blood cells that engulf pathogens rely on which organelle to destroy them?
Which organelle is produced by the Golgi apparatus and carries enzymes for intracellular digestion?

questions.why: Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs containing digestive enzymes that break down waste, worn-out organelles, and engulfed pathogens.
questions.deep: Memory aid: Lysosome = Lysis (to break apart). Ribosomes build proteins, the Golgi apparatus modifies and packages them, mitochondria make ATP. Lysosomes are especially abundant in phagocytic white blood cells.

variants.stem: How many valence electrons does an atom of chlorine (Group 17) have?
Fluorine, chlorine, and bromine are in Group 17. How many electrons are in the outer shell of each of these atoms?
Iodine is in Group 17. How many electrons does an iodine atom have in its outermost energy level?
An element in Group 17 needs one more electron to fill its outer shell. How many valence electrons does it currently have?
How many valence electrons does any halogen atom have?
Bromine is a halogen. How many electrons does one bromine atom have in its valence shell?
For Groups 13 to 18, the last digit of the group number equals the number of valence electrons. How many valence electrons are in an atom of Group 17?
How many valence electrons does an element have if it sits in the column just left of the noble gases?

questions.why: Elements in Group 17 (the halogens) have 7 valence electrons, one short of a full outer shell of 8.
questions.deep: The group number is NOT the valence electron count for Groups 13–18; use the last digit (Group 17 → 7, Group 16 → 6, Group 1 → 1). Atoms are most stable with a full outer shell (octet), so halogens readily gain one electron to become 1− anions. Elements in the same group share valence electron count; elements in the same period share the number of electron shells.

variants.stem: Which compound is held together by ionic bonds?
Which compound forms when a metal atom transfers electrons to a nonmetal atom?
Which common household substance is an ionic compound?
Which compound is made of positively and negatively charged ions attracted to each other?
Which formula represents an ionic compound?
Which compound has a crystal lattice made of oppositely charged ions?
In which compound is the electronegativity difference between the bonded atoms large enough to transfer electrons completely?
Which compound is formed from a metal and a nonmetal?

questions.why: NaCl forms when sodium (a metal) transfers an electron to chlorine (a nonmetal), creating Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held together by ionic bonds.
questions.deep: Rule of thumb: metal + nonmetal = ionic (electrons transferred); nonmetal + nonmetal = covalent (electrons shared). Ionic compounds form crystal lattices, have high melting points, and conduct electricity when dissolved in water or melted.

variants.stem: Select all that apply: Which of the following are ionic compounds?
Select all that apply: Which compounds are formed by a metal bonding with a nonmetal?
Select all that apply: Which substances consist of ions held together by electrostatic attraction?
Select all that apply: Which of these are covalent compounds (NOT ionic)?
Select all that apply: Which formulas represent ionic compounds?
Select all that apply: Which compounds would be expected to form a crystal lattice of cations and anions?
Select all that apply: Which compounds form when electrons are transferred from one atom to another?
Select all that apply: Which of the following are ionic?

questions.why: Ionic compounds form between a metal and a nonmetal through electron transfer (for example NaCl, MgO, CaCl₂). Compounds made only of nonmetals share electrons and are covalent.
questions.deep: Quick test: look for a metal (Groups 1, 2, or transition metals) paired with a nonmetal. Water, carbon dioxide, methane, and ammonia are covalent molecules. Ionic compounds conduct electricity when dissolved; molecular compounds generally do not.

variants.stem: What is formed when a neutral atom loses one or more electrons?
A sodium atom loses one electron to become Na⁺. What type of ion is Na⁺?
Which type of ion carries a positive charge?
Metals tend to lose electrons when they form ions. What are the resulting ions called?
An atom ends up with more protons than electrons. What is it called?
Ca²⁺ is classified as which type of ion?
Which particle would be attracted to the negative electrode (cathode) in an electric field?
When magnesium loses two electrons, the resulting positively charged particle is called a(n):

questions.why: Losing electrons leaves an atom with more protons than electrons, giving it a net positive charge. A positively charged ion is called a cation.
questions.deep: Memory aid: cATion = posiTIVE (the 't' looks like a plus sign) and Anion = A Negative ION. Metals usually form cations; nonmetals usually form anions by gaining electrons. Cations migrate toward the cathode.

variants.stem: According to the Arrhenius definition, an acid is a substance that releases which ion in water?
Which ion increases in concentration when an acid is dissolved in water?
A solution with a pH of 2 has a higher concentration of which ion than a solution with a pH of 9?
When HCl dissolves in water, which ion is responsible for the acidic properties of the solution?
Bases release hydroxide ions (OH⁻) in water. Acids, in contrast, release which ion?
Lemon juice is acidic because it contains a high concentration of which ion?
In the Brønsted–Lowry model, an acid is a proton donor. What is the proton that it donates?
A strong acid dissociates almost completely in water, producing many of which ion?

questions.why: Acids release hydrogen ions (H⁺) in water; the more H⁺, the lower the pH and the stronger the acidity.
questions.deep: Acids: release H⁺ (pH below 7). Bases: release OH⁻ (pH above 7). Memory aid: Acids Add H⁺. Each pH unit is a tenfold change in H⁺ concentration, so pH 2 has 10,000 times more H⁺ than pH 6.

variants.stem: A sodium atom has an atomic number of 11 and a mass number of 23. How many neutrons does it have?
An atom has 11 protons and a mass number of 23. How many neutrons are in its nucleus?
The nucleus of an atom contains 11 protons and has a total of 23 nucleons (protons plus neutrons). How many neutrons are present?
Sodium-23 has an atomic number of 11. How many neutrons does an atom of sodium-23 contain?
An atom's mass number is 23 and its atomic number is 11. Find its number of neutrons.
A neutral atom has 11 electrons and a mass number of 23. How many neutrons does it have?
In the notation ²³₁₁Na, how many neutrons are in the nucleus?
A nuclide has 11 protons, 11 electrons, and a mass number of 23. How many neutrons does it have?

questions.why: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23 − 11 = 12.
questions.deep: Atomic number = number of protons (and electrons in a neutral atom). Mass number = protons + neutrons. Isotopes of the same element have the same atomic number but different mass numbers (different numbers of neutrons).

variants.stem: What is the main purpose of a control group in an experiment?
opts: To provide a baseline for comparison
To receive the treatment being tested
To increase the total sample size
To prove that the hypothesis is true

variants.stem: A researcher tests a fertilizer on one set of plants and gives another set none. Why is the second set included?
opts: To show growth without the fertilizer
To grow taller than the treated plants
To test a second fertilizer brand
To save time during the experiment

variants.stem: Why do scientists keep a group that does not receive the experimental treatment?
opts: To compare against the treated group
To remove all sources of error

variants.stem: In a drug trial, one group receives a placebo instead of the medication. What role does this group play?
opts: It serves as the control group
It serves as the experimental group

variants.stem: Which statement best describes the function of a control group?
opts: It is the standard for comparing results
It receives every treatment at once
It is the variable the researcher changes
It is the data collected at the end

variants.stem: If the control group is removed from an experiment, what becomes hard to judge?
opts: Whether the treatment had an effect

variants.stem: A control group is treated like the experimental group in every way except one. What is its purpose?
opts: To isolate the effect of the variable
To increase the number of variables

variants.stem: Why do researchers compare experimental results with a control group?
opts: To see if the variable caused the change

questions.why: The control group does not receive the tested treatment, so it shows what happens without it and gives a baseline against which the experimental group is compared.
questions.deep: Everything except the independent variable is kept the same between the control and experimental groups. Without a control, you cannot tell whether a change was caused by the treatment or by something else. A placebo group is a common type of control.

variants.stem: A student tests how the number of hours of sunlight per day affects the height of bean plants. Which is the dependent variable?
A student grows bean plants under different amounts of daily sunlight and measures their heights after two weeks. Which variable is the outcome being measured?
In an experiment on how daily sunlight affects bean plant height, the researcher changes the sunlight. Which variable responds to that change?
Bean plants receive 4, 8, or 12 hours of light per day and their growth is compared. Which variable depends on the amount of light?
A student sets the hours of sunlight bean plants receive each day and records how tall the plants grow. Which quantity is observed and recorded rather than set?
A graph shows how sunlight hours affect bean plant growth, with sunlight hours on the x-axis. Which variable belongs on the y-axis?
If the hours of sunlight that bean plants receive are changed, which variable is expected to change as a result?
A student varies the light exposure of bean plants. To see the effect, the student measures which variable?

questions.why: The dependent variable is the outcome that is measured and that responds to the change; here, plant height responds to the hours of sunlight (the independent variable).
questions.deep: Independent variable = what the researcher changes (x-axis). Dependent variable = what is measured (y-axis). Controlled variables (seed type, soil, water, temperature) are kept the same. Memory aid: the Dependent variable Depends on the independent variable.

variants.stem: A measurement or experiment is described as reliable if it:
opts: Is close to the true value

variants.stem: Which situation best describes high reliability in an experiment?
opts: Repeated trials give nearly the same results
The results match the researcher's prediction
The experiment has a very large sample
The experiment was published in a journal

variants.stem: A scale reads 5.01 g, 5.00 g, and 5.02 g each time the same object is weighed. What does this indicate about the scale?
opts: It is reliable because the readings are consistent
It is accurate because it equals the true value
It is invalid because the readings differ

variants.stem: Which term describes how consistently an experiment's results can be reproduced?
Different researchers repeat an experiment and obtain the same results. This shows that the experiment is:
Which practice does the most to improve the reliability of results?
Which describes a reliable test?
opts: One that measures what it claims
One that uses the newest tools

variants.stem: A thermometer gives the same reading each time it is placed in the same water. Which quality is demonstrated?

questions.why: Reliability means that results are consistent and repeatable when the same procedure is repeated.
questions.deep: Reliability = consistency (same result every time). Accuracy = closeness to the true value. Validity = measuring what you intend to measure. A tool can be reliable without being accurate (consistently off by the same amount). Repeated trials improve confidence in reliability.
